title: JavaScript & TypeScript
blurb: The JS runtime model, async, the type system, and typing React code.

quiz.question: What does this print? console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2)); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); console.log(4);
quiz.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (1, 4), then the microtask queue (promise callback: 3), then the next macrotask (timer: 2).

quiz.question: What's the difference between let/const and var?
options: let/const are block-scoped and have a temporal dead zone; var is function-scoped and hoisted as undefined
quiz.explanation: let/const are block-scoped and can't be used before declaration (TDZ). var is function-scoped and initialized to undefined when hoisted. const only prevents rebinding, not mutation.

quiz.question: What is a closure?
options: A function bundled with references to the variables of the scope where it was created
A way to close a browser tab
quiz.explanation: A closure keeps access to its outer scope's variables even after that scope has returned — the basis of module patterns, memoization and React hooks.

quiz.question: Which comparison is true?
quiz.explanation: Loose equality treats null and undefined as equal to each other only. NaN is never equal to itself (use Number.isNaN), and distinct arrays are different references.

quiz.question: Promise.allSettled differs from Promise.all because it…
options: Rejects as soon as one promise rejects
Waits for every promise and reports each one's status
quiz.explanation: Promise.all short-circuits on the first rejection; allSettled always resolves with {status, value|reason} for each input. Promise.race and Promise.any settle on the first result.

problems.title: Debounce
problems.prompt: Implement debounce(fn, ms) so a search box only calls the API after the user stops typing for ms milliseconds.
hints: Keep a timer in a closure
problems.solution: function debounce(fn, ms) { let t; return function (...args) { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), ms); }; } — each call resets the timer, so fn runs once, ms after the last call. Add a cancel method if callers need to abort.

problems.title: Run with a concurrency limit
problems.prompt: You have 100 URLs. Fetch them all, but never more than 5 at a time, and return results in the original order.
problems.solution: Create 5 async workers that loop: take the next index from a shared counter, await fetch(urls[i]), store the result at results[i]. Await Promise.all(workers). Order is preserved because results are written by index; wrap each fetch in try/catch (or use allSettled semantics) so one failure doesn't stop the pool.
